title: Local species occupancy followed about 8-14% of spatial thermal expectation in US birds and 13 shelf-fish surveys (1969-2024); a common occupancy rise made the warm-gain versus cold-loss asymmetry
abstract: Question: prior work split the weak space-for-time transfer of community thermal composition into warm-side gains (about 45-95% of expectation) and absent cold-side losses, and treated persistence of cold-affinity species as the main cause. Marine shelf communities were a counter-case. Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey (1,184 routes, 1969-78 to 2015-24, nClimGrid), 12 OceanAdapt fish surveys (1982-2020) and ICES North Sea IBTS Q1 (1985-94 to 2015-24), SST climatology from OISST and change from ERSSTv5, external OBIS x WOA23 thermal indices. Method: for each species-site, the expected occupancy change from cross-fitted spatial occupancy-temperature curves was compared with the observed change, separately for expected gains and losses, with a common logit occupancy shift removed; design-specific simulation calibrated attenuation; spatial-block bootstrap and random-effects pooling. Results: raw side ratios reproduced the asymmetry (birds 0.91 versus -0.44; fish 0.27 versus -0.25). A common occupancy rise (birds +0.18 logit; North Sea +0.32; Northeast US +0.38 to +0.51, mainly the 2009 vessel change) caused it. With the shift removed and calibrated, birds followed 0.14 (0.09-0.19) of expectation, gains 0.17 and losses 0.13; shelf fish followed 0.08 (0.02-0.14), gains 0.05 and losses 0.10. Northeast US and North Sea CTI ratios were 1.06-1.25, but this came mainly from species-wide trends, not local sorting (North Sea species-level 0.05). Conclusion: the gap is a general weak link between local occupancy change and local thermal expectation, on both sides; cold-side persistence is not a sufficient explanation, and gain-loss splits must remove common occupancy shifts. Limitations: presence only, surface temperature, one shift term per network, fishing not modelled, 8 of 13 marine designs with attenuation factors below 0.5.

Right: with a common logit occupancy shift removed and design calibration applied, gains and losses are both small in birds (BBS, 2 regions) and shelf fish (10 informative surveys). 95% random-effects intervals.

Calibrated species-level transfer for expected gains and losses in each network, with the design attenuation factor lambda. Grey labels: lambda below 0.3, not pooled. 95% spatial-block bootstrap intervals divided by lambda.

Community temperature index (CTI) ratio and its parts: observed, species-wide occupancy trends only, local site deviations only, and full local space-for-time tracking. High marine CTI ratios come mainly from species-wide trends.

We confirm Northeast US CTI ratios near 1 with OBIS indices, but species-level local transfer is lower and the North Sea CTI rise comes from species-wide trends.
Weak temporal transfer of spatial thermal gradients; we measure it at the species-site level in birds and 13 fish surveys.
Presence (membership) carries most of the spatial gradient; we therefore use occupancy as the response.
Small aligned share of occupancy change in birds; our corrected species-level transfer is about 14%.
Local warming did not direct bird colonisation; our local within-species slopes are near 0.06.
